debate.situation: You see friends buying homes and getting married, and you feel behind even though you are not sure you want those things. What you know is the feeling of lagging; what you do not know is whether it points to a hidden wish for those milestones, a reaction to watching peers move together, or both. That unknown is decisive, because the feeling alone cannot tell you which it is. Note that the sources cited below were not checked against the texts in this session, so the ideas are paraphrased from general knowledge of each book.

minds.title: The Status Critic
minds.concern: Whether the feeling of being behind measures a real desire or only your position in a group's shared scoreboard.
minds.author: Thorstein Veblen
minds.book: The Theory of the Leisure Class

minds.title: The Forecasting Skeptic
minds.concern: Whether anyone, including you, can reliably predict from the armchair what will or will not make them content.
minds.author: Daniel Gilbert

minds.title: The Experimenter
minds.concern: Finding out what you want through small, real tests rather than through more thinking.
minds.author: Herminia Ibarra

debate.speaker: The Status Critic
debate.text: Start with where the feeling lives. Nothing in it mentions wanting a house or a spouse; it only says others are ahead. That is a ranking sensation. Groups tend to adopt whatever the neighbors visibly have as the standard of a decent life, and you are being scored on a game you never joined.
debate.author: Thorstein Veblen
debate.book: The Theory of the Leisure Class
debate.basis: Basis: Thorstein Veblen, The Theory of the Leisure Class (1899), on emulation of the standards of one's peers; source not verified, so this is a paraphrase.

debate.speaker: The Forecasting Skeptic
debate.text: Careful, that story is too convenient. Your claim that you are not sure you want these things is also a prediction about your future self, and people forecast their own contentment badly. The nagging feeling might be a faint yes. Explaining it away as peer pressure is as unproven as obeying it.
debate.author: Daniel Gilbert
debate.basis: Basis: Daniel Gilbert, Stumbling on Happiness (2006), on errors in imagining future feelings; source not verified, so this is a paraphrase.

debate.speaker: The Experimenter
debate.text: You are both arguing from an armchair, which is the worst place to learn this. People rarely think their way to what they want; they try something and notice the reaction. Rent near a lively neighborhood, date seriously for a season, price a mortgage honestly. Cheap tests beat a perfect theory.
debate.author: Herminia Ibarra
debate.basis: Basis: Herminia Ibarra, Working Identity (2003), on learning who you are by trying things rather than introspecting; source not verified, so this is a paraphrase.

debate.speaker: The Status Critic
debate.text: I'll grant tests, but they get contaminated. If every trial is run with your friends watching, you will end up measuring how much their approval pleases you. Walk through an apartment thinking how it would look to them and you have collected data about the scoreboard, not about you.
debate.author: Thorstein Veblen
debate.book: The Theory of the Leisure Class
debate.basis: Basis: Thorstein Veblen, The Theory of the Leisure Class (1899), on consumption shaped by the opinion of others; source not verified, so this is a paraphrase.

debate.speaker: The Forecasting Skeptic
debate.text: Then design around it. Ask people who actually live this way what an ordinary Tuesday feels like, not the wedding day or the closing day. We overweight the vivid event and forget the routine. And I'll undercut my own advice: their Tuesdays are a starting guess for yours, not a verdict, because your tastes may differ.
debate.author: Daniel Gilbert
debate.basis: Basis: Daniel Gilbert, Stumbling on Happiness (2006), on asking people who have lived an experience instead of imagining it; source not verified, so this is a paraphrase.

debate.speaker: The Experimenter
debate.text: Good, so the tests should be about Tuesdays too, not ceremonies. I'd go further than Ibarra here: before each test, decide what result would change your mind. Otherwise any outcome gets read as proof of what you already believed, whether that is I'm free or I'm falling behind.
debate.author: Herminia Ibarra
debate.basis: Basis: Herminia Ibarra, Working Identity (2003), on small experiments; the pre-commitment idea is the mind's own extension. Source not verified.

debate.speaker: The Status Critic
debate.text: Here is a harder cut. Suppose a test comes back with I like it fine. That could be a real want or the scoreboard doing its work. One way to separate them: would you still want it if nobody ever learned you had it? Imagine it fully private and see what survives.
debate.author: Thorstein Veblen
debate.book: The Theory of the Leisure Class
debate.basis: Basis: Thorstein Veblen, The Theory of the Leisure Class (1899); the privacy test is the mind's own extension, not the author's. Source not verified.

debate.speaker: The Forecasting Skeptic
debate.text: That test proves too much. Almost nothing worth having is private; being known and witnessed by someone is much of what a marriage or a home gives. If every shared meaning counts as contamination, you have defined wanting out of existence. Social does not mean fake.
debate.author: Daniel Gilbert
debate.basis: Basis: Daniel Gilbert, Stumbling on Happiness (2006), on how much of happiness depends on other people; the application here is the mind's own. Source not verified.

debate.speaker: The Status Critic
debate.text: Accepted, and it narrows my claim. Wanting to be witnessed by one person is a want. Wanting to keep pace with a group is a ranking. They can feel identical from inside, so the useful question is which one is pulling you, not whether other people are involved.
debate.author: Thorstein Veblen
debate.book: The Theory of the Leisure Class
debate.basis: Basis: Thorstein Veblen, The Theory of the Leisure Class (1899), on emulation versus other motives; the distinction drawn is the mind's own. Source not verified.

debate.speaker: The Experimenter
debate.text: Which also splits the problem in two. Feeling behind is one question; do you want this life is another. A test can answer the second while the first fades on its own. And if a season of trying shows no pull, doing nothing is a legitimate result, not a failure to act.
debate.author: Herminia Ibarra
debate.basis: Basis: Herminia Ibarra, Working Identity (2003), on testing possibilities before committing; the two-question split is the mind's own. Source not verified.

debate.clearer: The main insight is that two questions were tangled together: the feeling of being behind, which measures comparison with a group, and whether you want these particular things, which only experience can answer. Still disputed is how far the wish to be witnessed by others counts as your own want versus borrowed pressure, and whether your own doubt or your friends' reports are the better guide. A possible self-reflection: when you picture a home or a marriage, is it a specific ordinary day you are drawn to or repelled by, or mainly how it would look from outside? This is a question to try on, not a conclusion about you.
debate.dependsOn: If imagining ordinary days in these lives (not events) brings genuine pull, and small trials confirm it → pursuing one deliberately becomes more reasonable, because the feeling of being behind was pointing at a real want. If the pull appears mainly when you imagine friends' reactions, and ordinary-day trials feel flat → waiting or doing nothing becomes more reasonable, because the urgency is borrowed from the comparison. If it is unclear → run one or two cheap, reversible tests for a few months (talking with people about their routine weeks, a trial living or dating arrangement) and decide beforehand what outcome would count as a yes or a no. One more thing worth finding out: whether any option you care about has a real deadline, since some wants can wait indefinitely and others cannot.
